newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - For Latin American stars, all roads lead to Miami.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - For Latin American stars, all roads lead to Miami.

text.p: It's called "La Farandula" -- the glitzy, pulsating world of Latin American showbusiness.

But the soap opera stars, television personalities, singers and musicians who captivate millions from Mexico City to Buenos Aires are more than ever flocking to a U.S. city, Miami, to make their shows and discs. Record companies and Spanish-language cable TV companies based here make the Lincoln Road stretch of trendy Miami Beach a cross between Tin-Pan Alley and Hollywood.

"Miami is the uncontested entertainment capital of Latin America," said Xavier Roy, president of MIDEM (International Record, Music Publishing and Video Music Market). "Miami is the gateway between North and South America. It combines the romance of Latin America and the professionalism of the United States," he added, announcing that Miami will host a fair dedicated to Latin and Caribbean music next September.

The city's most famous songstress, Gloria Estefan, grew up here after her parents fled communist-ruled Cuba. She enjoys virtual deity status among the huge Cuban population and is probably the best known Hispanic entertainer to audiences outside the Spanish-speaking world.

Her husband Emilio's Crescent Moon studio nurtures Latin talent and their restaurant Larios on the Beach -- styled like an old Cuban night club -- is a popular hangout for the Farandula constellation.

Other Latin Americans have boosted their careers by coming to Miami after already tasting success at home. Last month, cable network CBS Telenoticias signed Peruvian Jaime Bayly, described by the Miami Herald as "one of Spanish-language television's most engaging personalities," to host a live nightly talk show.

The first edition of "En Directo con Jaime Bayly" goes out on Telenoticias on Nov. 18, one shot in the war shaping up for potentially vast cable markets in Latin America. Telenoticias President Francisco de la Torre estimates it will reach 14 million homes in the Americas and Spain, where Bayly is already a familiar face.
"It's like the Larry King show," Bayly told Reuters. "We will have phone calls from viewers. When I'm sitting in Miami I'm going to reach 21 countries. It's a big step forward in my career."
Miami was the logical place for him to come from Peru in 1995 to widen his audience, he said. "Miami is a cosmopoliton city in which no Latin American is a stranger."
Communications and facilities are excellent, he added.

The Saturday night variety show Sabado Gigante is also shot in Miami. A campy show hosted by Chilean Don Francisco, it has everything from dance contests to dwarves and is hugely popular with the U.S. Hispanic population as well as viewers in the southern continent.
Other TV operations headquartered here are Telemundo, Univision, and MTV Latino.

Recently Ya TV, owned by Warner and the German company BMG, has joined them. "We are aiming for a more adult audience than MTV," producer Edmundo Bracho-Polanco told Reuters. "Mexico and Argentina are the main markets but the operation is Miami-made and Miami-based. This is the melting pot."

Miami is also home to the Latin American divisions of several big music companies including Sony Discos, WEA Latina and PolyGram Latino. Salsa, merengue, samba and other Latin music styles are going through a boom period, driven in part by a younger and more affluent population in Latin America and by the rise of the World Music scene in Europe.

The venerable Criteria studio, where Aretha Franklin, the Bee Gees and Eric Clapton all cut classic records, now is used by many Latin artists. "It's been a gradual process over the past several years," studio manager Trevor Fletcher said.

Miami offers a wealth of support services including songwriters, producers, musicians and arrangers, he told Reuters, adding, "If you need an engineer that speaks Portuguese, you'll find him. If you need an arranger who's familiar with tango you'll find someone of Argentinian blood."

The technology is also better. In Latin American cities studio equipment is often years behind, Fletcher said. "Miami's bilingual, flights from South America are easy. And a person can come up here and relax."

It would be wrong, however, to assume Miami had created a homogenous Latin American popular culture, Brancho said. "Mexican humour is different to Chilean humour. There's no black culture at all in Argentina."
Soap operas made in Miami sometimes feature a bewildering array of actors, he said. "You get the mother speaking with a Mexican accent and the son speaking with a Cuban accent. It's funny."
